stimuli.title: Seven persons facing south, with home cities
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abhiraj, Charvi, Hriday, Kesha, Navya, Rishit and Tanmay sit in a straight row, all facing south. Each of them is from a different city among Agra, Bhopal, Indore, Kochi, Madurai, Patna and Surat. (For a person facing south, the right is towards the west and the left is towards the east.)

- Abhiraj sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Charvi sits second to the left of Abhiraj.
- The person from Bhopal sits immediately to the left of Charvi.
- Navya sits immediately to the right of Abhiraj.
- Kesha sits at one of the extreme ends of the row, but she is not from Bhopal.
- Tanmay sits immediately to the left of Abhiraj.
- Rishit is not from Bhopal.
- The person from Surat sits at the extreme right end of the row.
- Navya is from Kochi, and the person from Patna sits immediately to the left of Navya.
- Only one person sits between the persons from Agra and Kochi.
- Charvi is not from Indore.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 7 from the west end. Facing south, 'to the right' means a lower seat number and 'to the left' a higher one.
Step 1: Abhiraj = 4. Charvi is second to his left: 6. Navya is immediately to his right: 3, and Tanmay immediately to his left: 5.
Step 2: Bhopal is immediately to Charvi's left: seat 7. Kesha is at an end but not from Bhopal, so Kesha = 1.
Step 3: Seats 2 and 7 remain for Hriday and Rishit. Rishit is not from Bhopal (seat 7), so Rishit = 2 and Hriday = 7 (Bhopal).
Step 4: The extreme right end is the west end, seat 1: Kesha is from Surat. Navya (3) is from Kochi, and Patna is immediately to her left, seat 4: Abhiraj.
Step 5: Agra is two seats from Kochi (3): seat 1 or 5; seat 1 is Surat, so Agra = 5 (Tanmay). Indore and Madurai remain for Rishit and Charvi; Charvi is not from Indore, so Charvi is from Madurai and Rishit from Indore.

| Seat (from west) | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kesha | Surat |
| 2 | Rishit | Indore |
| 3 | Navya | Kochi |
| 4 | Abhiraj | Patna |
| 5 | Tanmay | Agra |
| 6 | Charvi | Madurai |
| 7 | Hriday | Bhopal |

stimuli.title: Eight persons facing north or south, with languages
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Advait, Bhairavi, Dhruv, Gargee, Jivesh, Kalyani, Paras and Sumedha sit in a straight row. Some of them face north and the others face south. Each of them is learning a different language among Bengali, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Spanish and Tamil. (For a person facing north, the right is towards the east; for a person facing south, the right is towards the west.)

- Sumedha learns German. She sits fourth from the west end of the row and faces north.
- Dhruv sits third to the right of Sumedha.
- Kalyani sits at one of the extreme ends of the row, and Dhruv sits immediately to her right.
- Paras sits at the other extreme end and faces the same direction as Kalyani.
- Bhairavi sits second to the right of Kalyani.
- Both persons sitting immediately next to Bhairavi face north, but Bhairavi does not.
- Jivesh sits immediately to the right of Sumedha.
- Advait sits second to the left of Jivesh.
- Gargee faces the same direction as Sumedha.
- Exactly four persons face north.
- Bhairavi learns Bengali. The person who learns Russian sits at an extreme end, and only one person sits between the Russian learner and Bhairavi.
- The Spanish learner sits immediately to the right of the German learner.
- Dhruv learns Japanese, and the French learner sits at an extreme end of the row.
- The Korean learner faces south.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 8 from the west end.
Step 1: Sumedha = 4, facing north, German. Dhruv is third to her right (east): 7.
Step 2: Dhruv is immediately to the right of Kalyani, who is at an end. Kalyani = 8 facing south (her right is west, seat 7) works; Kalyani = 1 cannot have seat 7 next to her. Paras = 1, facing south.
Step 3: Bhairavi is second to Kalyani's right: 8 − 2 = 6. Her neighbours (5 and 7) face north and she faces south, so Dhruv faces north.
Step 4: Jivesh is immediately to Sumedha's right: 5 (so he faces north). Jivesh faces north, so his left is west: Advait = 5 − 2 = 3, and Gargee takes seat 2.
Step 5: Gargee faces north like Sumedha. North-facing so far: Sumedha, Dhruv, Jivesh, Gargee = four, so Advait faces south.
Step 6: Russian is at an end two seats from Bhairavi (6): seat 8, Kalyani. Spanish is immediately right of German (seat 4, facing north): seat 5, Jivesh. Dhruv learns Japanese; French is at an end: seat 1, Paras.
Step 7: Korean and Tamil remain for Gargee (north) and Advait (south). The Korean learner faces south: Advait learns Korean and Gargee Tamil.

| Seat (from west) | Person | Faces | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Paras | south | French |
| 2 | Gargee | north | Tamil |
| 3 | Advait | south | Korean |
| 4 | Sumedha | north | German |
| 5 | Jivesh | north | Spanish |
| 6 | Bhairavi | south | Bengali |
| 7 | Dhruv | north | Japanese |
| 8 | Kalyani | south | Russian |

stimuli.title: A south-facing row of unknown length
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing south. (For a person facing south, the right is towards the west and the left is towards the east.) The number of persons in the row is not given. Ojasvi, Pratyush, Ranjana, Shailesh, Uditi and Varenya are among them.

- Ranjana sits fifth from the right end of the row.
- Shailesh sits sixth to the left of Ranjana.
- Only three persons sit between Shailesh and Uditi, and Uditi sits to the left of Shailesh.
- Varenya sits exactly midway between Ranjana and Uditi.
- Ojasvi sits second to the right of Varenya.
- Pratyush sits at the extreme left end of the row, and as many persons sit between Uditi and Pratyush as sit between Ranjana and Ojasvi.
stimuli.solution:
Count positions from the right end of the row (the west end, since everyone faces south). Moving 'to the left' of someone increases this count.
Step 1: Ranjana = 5th from the right. Shailesh is sixth to her left: 5 + 6 = 11th.
Step 2: Three persons sit between Shailesh and Uditi, Uditi on his left: 11 + 4 = 15th.
Step 3: Varenya is midway between 5th and 15th: 10th. Ojasvi is second to Varenya's right: 10 − 2 = 8th.
Step 4: Between Ranjana (5th) and Ojasvi (8th) sit two persons, so two persons sit between Uditi (15th) and Pratyush, who is at the left end: Pratyush = 15 + 3 = 18th from the right. The row has 18 persons.

| Person | From the right end | From the left end |
|---|---|---|
| Ranjana | 5th | 14th |
| Ojasvi | 8th | 11th |
| Varenya | 10th | 9th |
| Shailesh | 11th | 8th |
| Uditi | 15th | 4th |
| Pratyush | 18th | 1st |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six favourite colours
stimuli.content:
Six persons Kavin, Lajja, Mrinalini, Nimit, Pooja and Suhas live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 6 the topmost. Each of them likes a different colour among Blue, Green, Orange, Pink, Purple and Yellow.

- Kavin lives on floor 3.
- Only one person lives between Kavin and Lajja, and Lajja lives above Kavin.
- Mrinalini lives immediately above Lajja.
- The person who likes Green lives immediately below Lajja.
- Suhas lives above Pooja, and Nimit does not live on an even-numbered floor.
- The person who likes Pink lives on the topmost floor.
- The person who likes Purple lives immediately below the person who likes Green.
- Pooja likes Blue.
- The person who likes Yellow lives on an odd-numbered floor below Kavin.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kavin = 3, Lajja = 5, Mrinalini = 6.
Step 2: Floors 1, 2 and 4 remain for Nimit, Pooja and Suhas. Nimit is on an odd floor: 1. Suhas is above Pooja: Pooja = 2, Suhas = 4.
Step 3: Green is immediately below Lajja: floor 4 (Suhas). Purple is immediately below Green: floor 3 (Kavin). Pink is on floor 6 (Mrinalini). Pooja likes Blue.
Step 4: Yellow is on an odd floor below Kavin: floor 1 (Nimit). Orange is left for Lajja.

| Floor | Person | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Mrinalini | Pink |
| 5 | Lajja | Orange |
| 4 | Suhas | Green |
| 3 | Kavin | Purple |
| 2 | Pooja | Blue |
| 1 | Nimit | Yellow |

stimuli.title: Eight persons on eight floors
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Akhil, Bansi, Chinu, Darpan, Eela, Falgun, Gopi and Himani live on the eight floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 8 the topmost.

- Chinu lives immediately above Eela, and Gopi lives immediately below Eela.

Step 2: Chinu = 5 and Gopi = 3. Bansi is two floors above Chinu: 7.
Step 3: Akhil is on an even floor below 4: floor 2.
Step 4: Floors 1 and 6 remain for Falgun and Himani; Himani is above Falgun: Himani = 6, Falgun = 1.

stimuli.title: Seven floors and seven family sizes
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Jairam, Kumud, Madhav, Oorja, Pawan, Rachit and Shruti live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Their families have 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 members, a different number for each person.

- Shruti lives on floor 4, and Pawan lives immediately below her. Shruti's family has twice as many members as Pawan's.
- Madhav lives on the topmost floor, and his family has one member more than Pawan's.
- Only one person lives between Madhav and Jairam, and Jairam's family is the smallest of all.
- Oorja lives immediately below Madhav. Her family has as many members as Jairam's and Rachit's families together.
- Kumud lives above Rachit.
- The family on floor 2 is the largest of all.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Shruti = 4, Pawan = 3, Madhav = 7, Oorja = 6. Jairam is two floors from Madhav: 5. Kumud and Rachit take floors 2 and 1; Kumud is above Rachit, so Kumud = 2, Rachit = 1.
Step 2: Jairam's family is the smallest: 2. Kumud (floor 2) has the largest family: 8.
Step 3: Shruti = 2 × Pawan and Madhav = Pawan + 1. From 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 the only doubling pair is 3 and 6, so Pawan = 3, Shruti = 6, Madhav = 4.
Step 4: 5 and 7 remain for Oorja and Rachit, and Oorja = 2 + Rachit: Rachit = 5, Oorja = 7.

| Floor | Person | Family members |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Madhav | 4 |
| 6 | Oorja | 7 |
| 5 | Jairam | 2 |
| 4 | Shruti | 6 |
| 3 | Pawan | 3 |
| 2 | Kumud | 8 |
| 1 | Rachit | 5 |

stimuli.title: Eight floors, eight professions and eight home cities
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Amolika, Bhargav, Chandan, Damayanti, Girish, Hamida, Jignesh and Kalpesh live on the eight floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 8 the topmost). Each has a different profession among Architect, Banker, Chef, Dentist, Engineer, Lawyer, Pilot and Teacher, and each is from a different city among Gaya, Jaipur, Kanpur, Mysuru, Nagpur, Pune, Ranchi and Shimla.

- The Architect lives on the lowermost floor, and exactly three persons live between the Architect and the Lawyer.
- The person from Jaipur lives immediately below the Lawyer.
- Girish lives on the topmost floor and is the Pilot. The Pilot lives two floors above the Chef.
- Hamida lives immediately below Girish, and the Dentist is from Shimla.
- Kalpesh lives immediately below Damayanti, and Damayanti lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- The Engineer lives on an odd-numbered floor, immediately below the Teacher.
- Chandan lives immediately above the Architect and is from Kanpur.
- Amolika is from Mysuru, and the person from Gaya lives somewhere below her.
- The person from Pune lives above the person from Shimla, and the person from Nagpur lives on an even-numbered floor.
- Bhargav is not the Architect.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Architect = 1, Lawyer = 5, Jaipur = 4. Girish = 8 and is the Pilot, so the Chef is on floor 6. Hamida = 7. Chandan = 2 (above the Architect), from Kanpur.
Step 2: Damayanti is on an odd floor with Kalpesh immediately below. Floor 1 has nothing below, floor 3 would need Kalpesh on Chandan's floor 2, and floor 7 is Hamida's, so Damayanti = 5 (Lawyer) and Kalpesh = 4 (Jaipur).
Step 3: The Engineer is on an odd floor immediately below the Teacher: floor 1 is the Architect and floor 7 would need the Teacher on the Pilot's floor 8, so Engineer = 3 and Teacher = 4 (Kalpesh).
Step 4: Banker and Dentist remain for floors 2 and 7. The Dentist is from Shimla, but floor 2 is Kanpur, so Dentist = 7 (Hamida, Shimla) and Banker = 2 (Chandan). Pune is above Shimla: floor 8.
Step 5: Amolika, Bhargav and Jignesh take floors 1, 3 and 6; Gaya, Mysuru, Nagpur and Ranchi go to floors 1, 3, 5 and 6. Nagpur is on an even floor: 6. Amolika is from Mysuru with Gaya below her, so she is not on 1 or 6: Amolika = 3 (Mysuru), Gaya = 1 and Ranchi = 5. Bhargav is not the Architect: Bhargav = 6, Jignesh = 1.

| Floor | Person | Profession | City |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | Girish | Pilot | Pune |
| 7 | Hamida | Dentist | Shimla |
| 6 | Bhargav | Chef | Nagpur |
| 5 | Damayanti | Lawyer | Ranchi |
| 4 | Kalpesh | Teacher | Jaipur |
| 3 | Amolika | Engineer | Mysuru |
| 2 | Chandan | Banker | Kanpur |
| 1 | Jignesh | Architect | Gaya |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes with weights and colours
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes C, G, K, N, Q, U and Z are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 7 the top). Their weights are 12, 15, 18, 22, 26, 30 and 35 kg, and their colours are Black, Brown, Cream, Gold, Maroon, Silver and Violet, one weight and one colour per box.

- Box C is kept exactly in the middle of the stack, and Box Q is kept immediately above Box C.
- Box N is kept at the top. It is 4 kg heavier than Box C.
- Exactly three boxes are kept between Box N and Box Z.
- Box Z is the heaviest box, and its colour is Gold.
- Box K is kept immediately below Box Z and is the lightest box.
- Box U is kept below Box G.
- Box Q is twice as heavy as Box G.
- The Silver box is kept at the bottom, and it weighs 26 kg.
- The Black box is the lightest box.
- The Violet box is kept immediately between the Gold box and the Brown box.
- The Cream box is lighter than the Maroon box.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: C = 4, Q = 5, N = 7. Three boxes lie between N and Z: Z = 3 (Gold, 35 kg). K = 2 (12 kg, so Black).
Step 2: Positions 1 and 6 remain for U and G; U is below G: U = 1, G = 6. The Silver box is at the bottom and weighs 26 kg: U.
Step 3: Weights left: 15, 18, 22, 30 for C, G, N, Q. N = C + 4 gives 18 and 22; Q = 2 × G gives 15 and 30. So C = 18, N = 22, G = 15, Q = 30.
Step 4: Violet lies between Gold (3) and Brown with one box between them, so Brown = 5 (Q) and Violet = 4 (C). Cream and Maroon remain for G (15 kg) and N (22 kg); Cream is lighter: G Cream, N Maroon.

| Position | Box | Weight (kg) | Colour |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | N | 22 | Maroon |
| 6 | G | 15 | Cream |
| 5 | Q | 30 | Brown |
| 4 | C | 18 | Violet |
| 3 | Z | 35 | Gold |
| 2 | K | 12 | Black |
| 1 | U | 26 | Silver |

stimuli.title: Nine boxes in a three-by-three rack
stimuli.content:
A rack has three shelves (top, middle and bottom), and each shelf has three compartments (left, middle and right, as seen from the front). Nine boxes D, E, G, I, M, O, R, U and W are kept in the rack, one in each compartment. 'Directly above/below' means in the same column on the next shelf.

- Box U is kept in the centre compartment of the rack (middle shelf, middle column).
- Box M is kept directly below Box U.
- Box E is kept immediately to the right of Box M, on the same shelf.
- Box I is kept directly above Box E.
- Box G is kept immediately to the left of Box O, on the same shelf.
- Box D is kept directly below Box W.
- Box R is kept on the bottom shelf.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: U = middle shelf, middle. M is directly below: bottom, middle. E is to M's right: bottom, right. I is directly above E: middle, right.
Step 2: Free compartments: bottom-left, middle-left and the whole top shelf. R is on the bottom shelf: bottom-left.
Step 3: D is directly below W, and only the left column has two free compartments one above the other (middle-left and top-left): D = middle-left, W = top-left.
Step 4: G and O take the top-middle and top-right compartments, G on the left.

| Shelf | Left | Middle | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | W | G | O |
| Middle | D | U | I |
| Bottom | R | M | E |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes and the sums of their weights
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes F, J, K, P, S, T, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Their weights are 6, 9, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23 and 27 kg, one weight per box.

- Box S is kept fifth from the bottom.
- The heaviest box is kept two places below Box S, and the lightest box is kept immediately below Box S.
- Exactly three boxes are kept between Box P and the heaviest box, and Box P is kept above it.
- Box K is kept between Box S and Box P.
- Box V is kept at the top, and its weight equals the combined weight of Box F and Box P.
- Box K weighs as much as Box S and Box J together.
- Box J is kept immediately above Box T, and Box T is lighter than Box Y.
- The two bottom boxes together weigh 29 kg.
- Box P is lighter than Box V but heavier than Box J.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: S = 5. The heaviest box (27 kg) is at 3 and the lightest (6 kg) at 4. P is four places above the heaviest: P = 7. K lies between S and P: K = 6. V = 8. F, J, T and Y take positions 1 to 4.
Step 2: 9, 11, 14, 17, 20 and 23 kg are left for positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 and 8. The two bottom boxes weigh 29 kg together: only 9 + 20 works, so positions 1 and 2 hold 9 and 20 kg, and S, K, P, V share 11, 14, 17, 23.
Step 3: K = S + J, where J is one of the bottom four (9, 20, 27 or 6 kg). The possibilities are 14 + 9 = 23 or 11 + 6 = 17 or 17 + 6 = 23. V = F + P with P lighter than V uses the other two weights: (a) S 14, J 9, K 23 ⇒ V 17, P 11, F 6; (b) S 11, J 6, K 17 ⇒ V 23, P 14, F 9; (c) S 17, J 6, K 23 ⇒ V 14, P 11, F 3 ✗.
Step 4: In (b) J (6 kg) is at 4, so T is at 3 with 27 kg and Y would be lighter than T ✗. So (a): F = 4 (6 kg); J (9 kg) is in the bottom pair and is immediately above T: T = 1 (20 kg), J = 2, and Y = 3 (27 kg). P (11) is heavier than J (9) and lighter than V (17), as required.

| Position | Box | Weight (kg) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | V | 17 |
| 7 | P | 11 |
| 6 | K | 23 |
| 5 | S | 14 |
| 4 | F | 6 |
| 3 | Y | 27 |
| 2 | J | 9 |
| 1 | T | 20 |

stimuli.title: Five arrow symbols for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, arrows are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ↑ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ↓ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ⇑ B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A ⇓ B' means 'A is not greater than B'; 'A ↔ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ↑ means >, ↓ means <, ⇑ means ≥ ('not smaller than'), ⇓ means ≤ ('not greater than') and ↔ means =. Rewrite every statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain and test each conclusion along it.

stimuli.title: Six morning runners and their distances
stimuli.content:
Six friends Amol, Binita, Chirag, Deepti, Eshan and Gargi each ran a different distance on a Sunday morning.

- Deepti ran farther than Chirag but less than Gargi.
- Amol ran less than Chirag.
- Eshan ran farther than Gargi.
- Binita ran farther than Amol but less than Chirag.
stimuli.solution: Chirag < Deepti < Gargi < Eshan, and Amol < Binita < Chirag. Joined: Eshan > Gargi > Deepti > Chirag > Binita > Amol.

stimuli.title: Seven bank officers: designations and review days
stimuli.content:
Seven officers Ansh, Bina, Chhavi, Darsh, Eshita, Faisal and Gita of a bank hold seven different designations. In decreasing order of seniority these are: General Manager, Deputy General Manager, Assistant General Manager, Chief Manager, Senior Manager, Manager and Officer. Each officer conducts a review on a different day of one week, from Monday to Sunday.

- The General Manager's review is on Thursday.
- Darsh is the Assistant General Manager, and his review is on the day immediately after the Officer's review.
- Exactly two reviews are held between Bina's review and the General Manager's review, and Bina is junior to Darsh.
- Faisal's review is on Sunday. Faisal is senior to Chhavi but junior to Eshita.
- The Manager's review is on Monday.
- Gita's review is on the day immediately before Ansh's review, and Gita is senior to Ansh.
- Exactly one review is held between Ansh's review and Faisal's review.
- Ansh is senior to Eshita.
- Chhavi's review is earlier in the week than Darsh's review.
stimuli.solution:
Bina is three days away from the General Manager's Thursday: Monday or Sunday; Faisal has Sunday, so Bina is on Monday and, as the Monday reviewer, is the Manager. One review between Ansh and Faisal (Sunday) puts Ansh on Friday and Gita on Thursday, so Gita is the General Manager. Tuesday, Wednesday and Saturday remain for Chhavi, Darsh and Eshita. Darsh comes the day after the Officer: Darsh on Saturday would make Ansh (Friday) the Officer, but Ansh is senior to Eshita; Darsh on Tuesday would make the Monday Manager the Officer. So Darsh is on Wednesday and the Officer on Tuesday; Chhavi is earlier than Darsh, so Chhavi is on Tuesday (Officer) and Eshita on Saturday. Ranks left 2, 4, 5: Ansh > Eshita > Faisal gives Ansh DGM, Eshita Chief Manager, Faisal Senior Manager.

Mon Bina (Manager), Tue Chhavi (Officer), Wed Darsh (AGM), Thu Gita (GM), Fri Ansh (DGM), Sat Eshita (Chief Manager), Sun Faisal (Senior Manager).

stimuli.title: Digit codes for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode each expression pair by pair from the left, draw the small tree, and read the asked relation off it. A child of a married person is taken to be the child of the couple.

stimuli.title: A family of eight with three couples
stimuli.content:
A family has eight members: Anand, Bharati, Chinmay, Damini, Ekansh, Fatima, Gopal and Hema. There are exactly three married couples, and every married person's spouse is a member of the family. Anand is male.

- Anand and Bharati are married to each other and have exactly three children, of whom only one is a daughter.
- Damini is the daughter of Bharati and is unmarried.
- Ekansh, a boy, is the only grandchild of Anand, and Hema is Ekansh's mother.
- Chinmay is a son of Anand.
- Fatima is the wife of one of Ekansh's uncles.
- Gopal is not an uncle of Ekansh.
stimuli.solution:
Anand's children are Damini and two sons. Ekansh's mother Hema must be married to a son of Anand (Damini is unmarried). The only males left are Chinmay, Ekansh and Gopal, and Ekansh is a grandchild, so Anand's sons are Chinmay and Gopal. Gopal is not Ekansh's uncle, so he is Ekansh's father and Hema's husband; Fatima is then Chinmay's wife.
Tree: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh.

stimuli.title: Six places in a small town
stimuli.content:
Six places in a small town are located as follows.

- The temple is 12 km north of the market.
- The school is 5 km east of the temple.
- The hospital is 5 km west of the market.
- The post office is 6 km south of the temple.
- The library is 1 km east of the hospital.
stimuli.solution: Put the market at (0, 0), east and north positive: temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0).

stimuli.title: Four coded sentences about a train
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'train leaves early today' is written as 've ko ra mi'
'today platform is crowded' is written as 'tu mi ne sa'
'night train arrives today' is written as 'le zo mi ra'
'platform leaves at night' is written as 'pu sa zo ko'
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: today = mi (sentences 1, 2 and 3); train = ra (1 and 3); leaves = ko (1 and 4); platform = sa (2 and 4); night = zo (3 and 4). Leftovers: early = ve, arrives = le, at = pu. 'is' and 'crowded' appear only in sentence 2, so they share 'tu' and 'ne' in some order.

stimuli.title: Seven persons and their weights
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abha, Bimal, Charu, Dhruv, Ekta, Farhan and Gopi have different weights.

- Only two persons are heavier than Abha.
- Dhruv is heavier than Farhan but lighter than Charu.
- Exactly two persons have weights between those of Charu and Ekta.
- Charu is heavier than Ekta.
- Gopi is lighter than Farhan.
- Bimal is heavier than Dhruv, but Bimal is not the heaviest.
stimuli.solution: Abha is the 3rd heaviest. Gopi < Farhan < Dhruv < Charu, so Charu is at least 4th from the bottom, and Ekta is exactly three places below Charu. If Charu were 4th from the bottom, Ekta would be the lightest, but Gopi, Farhan and Dhruv must fill the three places below Charu. If Charu were 2nd heaviest, Ekta would be 5th heaviest, Dhruv 4th heaviest, and Bimal (heavier than Dhruv, not the heaviest) would have no place. So Charu is the heaviest, Ekta 4th, Bimal 2nd, and Dhruv, Farhan, Gopi follow. Heaviest to lightest: Charu, Bimal, Abha, Ekta, Dhruv, Farhan, Gopi.

stimuli.title: Machine: most consonants to the right end
stimuli.content:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word with the most consonants (letters other than a, e, i, o and u); if two such words have the same number of consonants, it takes the one that comes first in alphabetical order. It places that word at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already arranged there (in Step I, at the extreme right). The other words keep their order. The machine stops when the arrangement is complete.

Input: glints planet aroma stream oasis branch idea
stimuli.solution:
Consonants: planet 4, stream 4, oasis 2, branch 5, idea 1, glints 5, aroma 2. Order of selection: branch, glints, planet, stream, aroma, oasis, idea.

Step I: glints planet aroma stream oasis idea branch
Step II: planet aroma stream oasis idea glints branch
Step III: aroma stream oasis idea planet glints branch
Step IV: aroma oasis idea stream planet glints branch
Step V: oasis idea aroma stream planet glints branch
Step VI: idea oasis aroma stream planet glints branch

stimuli.title: Machine: numbers read backwards
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of two-digit numbers step by step. In each step it takes, among the numbers not yet arranged, the one whose value is the smallest when its digits are read in reverse order, writes it with its digits reversed, and places it immediately to the right of the numbers already arranged at the left end (in Step I, at the extreme left). The other numbers keep their order. The machine stops when every number has been arranged.

Input: 62 38 81 47 15 93

stimuli.title: Machine: swapped letters and units-digit numbers
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it makes two moves: (1) among the words not yet arranged, it takes the word with the fewest vowels (a, e, i, o, u; if two words have the same number of vowels, the one that comes first in alphabetical order), interchanges its first two letters, and places it at the left end, immediately to the right of the words already placed there; (2) among the numbers not yet arranged, it takes the one with the largest units digit, adds its units digit to it, and places the result at the right end, immediately to the left of the numbers already placed there. All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

stimuli.solution:
Words: brush (1 vowel), stick (1), then apron, garden, kite (2 each) → rbush, tsick, paron, agrden, ikte. Numbers by units digit: 89, 37, 45, 54, 62 → 98, 44, 50, 58, 64.

Step I: rbush garden 37 kite 54 apron 62 stick 45 98
Step II: rbush tsick garden kite 54 apron 62 45 44 98
Step III: rbush tsick paron garden kite 54 62 50 44 98
Step IV: rbush tsick paron agrden kite 62 58 50 44 98
Step V: rbush tsick paron agrden ikte 64 58 50 44 98

Eight persons Ishika, Jairaj, Kriti, Nakul, Pihu, Ritvik, Sanvi and Yashas sit in a straight row of eight seats, numbered 1 to 8 from the west end. - Ishika sits immediately to the right of Yashas, and Jairaj sits third to the right of Yashas.
- Sanvi sits immediately to the left of Jairaj.
- Yashas does not sit at an extreme end of the row, but Nakul does.

How many persons sit between Nakul and the person who sits immediately to the left of Pihu?

solution.concept: When the facing depends on the seat, check which half each person sits in before moving right or left
solution.explanation: Yashas faces south, so he is in seat 5, 6 or 7, and Ishika and Jairaj are one and three seats west of him. Only Yashas = 6 works, giving (west to east) Nakul, Sanvi, Jairaj, Pihu, Ishika, Yashas, Kriti, Ritvik. Pihu (seat 4) faces north, so her left is west: seat 3, Jairaj. Between Nakul (1) and Jairaj (3) sits one person.

Yashas 7 ⇒ Ishika 6, Jairaj 4 ⇒ Sanvi 3; Ritvik 8 needs Kriti 7 ✗, Ritvik 1 ⇒ Kriti 2, Nakul 8, Pihu 5 faces south ✗
Yashas 6 ⇒ Ishika 5, Jairaj 3 ⇒ Sanvi 2; Ritvik 1 needs Kriti 2 ✗ ⇒ Ritvik 8, Kriti 7, Nakul 1, Pihu 4 ✓
Pihu (4, north) ⇒ left = west = seat 3 = Jairaj

Chaitra = immediate right = seat 1
Bhumika = second to the left (two seats clockwise) = seat 3
Seats 2 and 4 remain; seat 2 touches Chaitra ⇒ Daman = 4, Eshwar = 2
Eshwar's neighbours: Chaitra (1) and Bhumika (3)

questions.question_text:
Six persons Kamakshi, Manohar, Neha, Omprakash, Prakriti and Rajat sit around a hexagonal table, one at each side, all facing away from the centre. (Facing outside, a person's right is the next seat clockwise.)

- Neha sits immediately to the right of Kamakshi.
- Rajat sits second to the left of Neha.

solution.explanation: Number the seats 0 to 5 anticlockwise from Kamakshi. Manohar = 3 (opposite). Neha is to Kamakshi's right, i.e. clockwise: seat 5. Rajat is second to Neha's left (anticlockwise): seat 1, and Prakriti is immediately to Rajat's left: seat 2. Omprakash takes seat 4. Two seats to his right (clockwise) is seat 2: Prakriti.
steps: Kamakshi 0, Manohar 3
Facing outside: right = clockwise ⇒ Neha = 5
Left = anticlockwise ⇒ Rajat = 5 + 2 = 1, Prakriti = 2
Omprakash = 4
Second to his right: 4 → 3 → 2 ⇒ Prakriti

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Ambika, Bhushan, Champa, Devesh, Gaurika, Harbhajan, Indrajit and Jyoti sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some face the centre and the others face outside, and of any two persons sitting next to each other, one faces the centre and the other faces outside. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)
- Ambika faces the centre, and Harbhajan sits exactly opposite her.
- Bhushan sits immediately to the left of Harbhajan.
- Jyoti sits immediately to the right of Bhushan.
- Indrajit faces the centre.
- Devesh is an immediate neighbour of Ambika.
- Gaurika sits second to the left of Champa.

Who sits third to the right of Indrajit?

solution.concept: With alternate facing, every second seat faces the same way
solution.explanation: Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise from Ambika. Ambika faces the centre, so even seats face the centre and odd seats face outside. Harbhajan = 4 (centre); his left is clockwise: Bhushan = 3 (outside). Bhushan's right is clockwise: Jyoti = 2. Indrajit faces the centre: the only even seat left is 6. Devesh, Champa and Gaurika take 1, 5 and 7; Gaurika is second to the left (anticlockwise) of an outside-facing Champa, which works only for Champa = 5, Gaurika = 7, leaving Devesh = 1, next to Ambika. Indrajit (6) faces the centre: three seats anticlockwise is seat 1, Devesh.
steps: Even seats face the centre, odd seats outside
Harbhajan 4 ⇒ Bhushan 3 ⇒ Jyoti 2
Indrajit = 6
Champa 5, Gaurika 7, Devesh 1
Third to Indrajit's right: 6 → 7 → 0 → 1 ⇒ Devesh
solution.why_others_wrong: Gaurika is immediately to Indrajit's right, Ambika second to his right, and Champa immediately to his left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Ten persons Anup, Bhanu, Deepika, Gyan, Hiten, Ira, Kanchan, Mihir, Nirmala and Purab sit around a rectangular table, all facing the centre. One person sits at each of the two shorter sides and four persons sit along each of the two longer sides, so that each person on a longer side sits directly opposite a person on the other longer side. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise.)
- Ira and Gyan sit at the two shorter sides.
- Mihir sits second to the right of Ira.
- Purab sits directly opposite Mihir.
- Deepika sits fourth to the left of Purab.
- Kanchan sits immediately between Mihir and Deepika.
- Hiten sits immediately to the left of Ira.
- Nirmala sits immediately to the right of Gyan.
- Bhanu does not sit next to Ira.

Who sits directly opposite Anup?

solution.concept: Number the seats round the table and pair the long-side seats
solution.explanation: Start at Ira's shorter side and number the seats 0 to 9 anticlockwise; Gyan is at seat 5. Seats 1–4 form one longer side and 9–6 the other, so seat s faces seat 10 − s. Mihir = 2, Purab opposite = 8, Deepika four seats clockwise from Purab = 4, Kanchan between them = 3, Hiten = 9 and Nirmala = 6. Bhanu cannot sit next to Ira, so Bhanu = 7 and Anup = 1. Seat 1 faces seat 9: Hiten.
steps: Ira 0, Gyan 5; seat s faces 10 − s
Mihir 2 ⇒ Purab 8 ⇒ Deepika 4 ⇒ Kanchan 3
Hiten 9 (Ira's left), Nirmala 6 (Gyan's right)
Seats 1, 7 for Anup, Bhanu; Bhanu not next to Ira ⇒ Anup 1
Opposite seat 1 = seat 9 ⇒ Hiten
solution.why_others_wrong: Bhanu faces Kanchan, Nirmala faces Deepika, and Purab faces Mihir.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Ten persons Aditi, Bipin, Dhanush, Gautam, Hansraj, Jasmeet, Laboni, Murali, Neelima and Sameer sit around a table shaped like a regular pentagon. Five of them sit at the five corners and face away from the centre; the other five sit at the middle of the five sides and face the centre. Corner and side seats alternate around the table. questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All herons are storks.
No stork is an egret.

Conclusions:
I. No heron is an egret.
II. Some egrets are herons.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Two-statement syllogism (Venn diagram method)
solution.explanation: Every heron lies inside the storks, and the storks lie completely outside the egrets, so no heron can be an egret: I follows. Because no heron is an egret, 'Some egrets are herons' is impossible: II does not follow.
steps: All herons are storks + No stork is an egret ⇒ No heron is an egret (All + No = No)
I follows; II contradicts I, so it does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some tractors are scooters.
Some scooters are jeeps.

Conclusions:
I. Some tractors are jeeps.
II. No tractor is a jeep.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.concept: Two-statement syllogism (Venn diagram method)
solution.explanation: Two 'Some' statements give no definite link between tractors and jeeps, so neither conclusion is certain on its own. But I and II are about the same pair and between them cover every case (either some tractors are jeeps or none is), so exactly one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: Some + Some ⇒ no definite conclusion
I and II: 'Some A are B' and 'No A is B' form a complementary pair
Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, so 'Only I' and 'Only II' are wrong; but in every diagram one of the two holds, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.concept: 'Only a few' and 'Only' statements
solution.explanation: 'Only a few ladles are sieves' means some ladles are sieves and some are not. The ladles that are sieves are also graters, so some graters are ladles (II). The ladles outside the sieves may or may not be graters, so 'All ladles are graters' is not certain (I).
steps: Ladle ∩ sieve ≠ ∅ and ⊂ graters ⇒ some graters are ladles: II follows
Ladles outside sieves are unrestricted ⇒ I not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion I is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only I' are wrong; II holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

solution.concept: 'Only a few' and 'Only' statements
solution.explanation: 'Only beavers are otters' means every otter is a beaver. The walruses that are otters are therefore beavers, so some beavers are walruses (I). Nothing stops the walrus circle from covering the whole otter circle, so 'All otters being walruses' is possible (II).

solution.why_others_wrong: Two misses Amol or Binita; Four counts Deepti herself; One counts only Amol.

questions.question_text: If the farthest runner covered 12 km and each runner covered exactly 1 km more than the next shorter runner, how far did Chirag run?

12, 11, 10, 9 ⇒ Chirag 9 km

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Harsh, Ila, Jai, Kriti and Lalit visit a dental clinic on five consecutive days from Thursday to the following Monday, one person per day.

- Ila visits on the day immediately before Kriti.
- Jai visits on the last of the five days.
- Lalit visits on a later day than Harsh.

Who visits on Sunday?

solution.concept: Days across a weekend
solution.explanation: Kriti is on Saturday and Ila on Friday. Jai takes the last day, Monday. Thursday and Sunday remain; Lalit is later than Harsh, so Harsh visits on Thursday and Lalit on Sunday.
steps: Kriti Sat, Ila Fri, Jai Mon
Thursday and Sunday left; Harsh before Lalit ⇒ Lalit Sunday
solution.why_others_wrong: Harsh visits on Thursday, Jai on Monday and Ila on Friday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five teachers Mehul, Nisha, Omkar, Priti and Rohan work in a college. Four of them hold the posts of Principal, Vice-Principal, Head of Department and Lecturer, one post each, in decreasing order of seniority.

- Priti is the Vice-Principal.
- Rohan holds a post junior to Priti's post but senior to Omkar's.
- Nisha is senior to Omkar.

Who is the Head of Department?

solution.concept: Seniority order of posts
solution.explanation: Mehul holds no post. Priti is the Vice-Principal. Rohan is junior to Priti but senior to Omkar, so Rohan is the Head of Department and Omkar the Lecturer. That leaves Nisha as Principal (senior to Omkar, as required).
steps: Mehul: no post; Priti: Vice-Principal
Priti > Rohan > Omkar ⇒ Rohan HoD, Omkar Lecturer
Nisha: Principal

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five teams Amber, Coral, Ivory, Jade and Ruby play a round-robin tournament: every team plays every other team exactly once, and every match has a winner (no draws). At the end, no two teams have won the same number of matches.
- Jade won more matches than Ruby but fewer than Ivory.
- Amber beat Ivory.
- Coral lost to Ruby.

How many matches did Jade win?

solution.concept: Distinct win counts in a round-robin
solution.explanation: There are 10 matches and each team plays 4. Five different win counts adding up to 10 must be 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0. Then the team with 4 wins beat everyone, the team with 3 beat all but the top team, and so on — a strict ladder. Ivory > Jade > Ruby in wins, Ruby beat Coral so Ruby is above Coral, and Amber beat Ivory so Amber is above Ivory. Ladder: Amber 4, Ivory 3, Jade 2, Ruby 1, Coral 0.
steps: 10 matches; distinct counts from 0–4 adding to 10 ⇒ 4, 3, 2, 1, 0
Distinct counts ⇒ higher team beats lower
Amber > Ivory > Jade > Ruby > Coral
Jade: 2 wins
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is Ivory's count, 1 Ruby's and 4 Amber's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six trainers Gauri, Hemant, Isha, Jairaj, Komal and Lakshay each take one session in a two-week course. Sessions are held only on Monday, Wednesday and Friday of each week (six sessions in all), one trainer per session.
- Isha's session is on the Wednesday of week 2.
- Exactly two sessions are held between Isha's session and Gauri's session.
- Komal's session is on a Friday.
- Hemant's session is in the same week as Komal's, and earlier.
- Lakshay's session is the first of the six.

Whose session is on the Friday of week 1?

solution.concept: Slots in order: Mon, Wed, Fri of week 1, then week 2
solution.explanation: Number the slots 1 to 6. Isha is slot 5; two sessions between Isha and Gauri puts Gauri in slot 2 (slot 8 does not exist). Lakshay is slot 1. Komal is on a Friday (slot 3 or 6) with Hemant earlier in the same week: slot 3 would need Hemant in slot 1 or 2, both taken, so Komal is slot 6 and Hemant slot 4 (slot 5 is Isha's). Jairaj takes the remaining slot 3, the Friday of week 1.
steps: Slots 1–6; Isha 5, Gauri 2, Lakshay 1
Komal Friday: slot 3 fails (Hemant has no room) ⇒ slot 6
Hemant slot 4
Jairaj slot 3 = Friday of week 1
solution.why_others_wrong: Hemant is on Monday of week 2, Gauri on Wednesday of week 1 and Komal on Friday of week 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Gauri's mother is the only sister of Hemant. Hemant's father is Vinod. How is Vinod related to Gauri?

solution.concept: A mother's father is a grandfather
solution.explanation: Gauri's mother is Hemant's sister, so she is also Vinod's daughter. Vinod is therefore the father of Gauri's mother: Gauri's (maternal) grandfather.
steps: Gauri's mother = Hemant's sister ⇒ Vinod's daughter
Father of one's mother ⇒ grandfather
solution.why_others_wrong: Father and Uncle put Vinod one generation too low; Father-in-law would need Gauri to be married to Vinod's son.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Nikhil is the only brother of Manoj. Lalita is Manoj's wife, and Ketan is Lalita's son. How is Ketan related to Nikhil?

solution.concept: A brother's son is a nephew
solution.explanation: Ketan is the son of Lalita and her husband Manoj. Manoj is Nikhil's brother, so Ketan is the son of Nikhil's brother: Nikhil's nephew.
steps: Ketan = son of Manoj (Lalita's husband)
Son of one's brother ⇒ nephew
solution.why_others_wrong: Ketan's father is Manoj, not Nikhil; Ketan is a generation below Nikhil, so he is neither his brother nor his cousin.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A is the child of B. B is the only son of C, and D is C's wife. How is D related to A?

solution.concept: The wife of a grandfather is a grandmother
solution.explanation: B is the son of C and his wife D, so D is B's mother. A is B's child, so D is A's grandmother (whether A is a boy or a girl).
steps: D = mother of B
A = child of B ⇒ D is A's grandmother
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother is D's relation to B; Aunt would need D to be a sister of A's parent; Mother-in-law would need A to be married to D's child.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Simran's husband is the brother of Tara. Tara's mother is Usha. How is Simran related to Usha?

solution.concept: A son's wife is a daughter-in-law
solution.explanation: Simran's husband is Tara's brother, so he is also Usha's son. Simran, the wife of Usha's son, is Usha's daughter-in-law.
steps: Simran's husband = Tara's brother = Usha's son
Son's wife ⇒ daughter-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Simran is not Usha's own child; she is Tara's sister-in-law, not Usha's; a niece is a sibling's daughter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Deepa's son Arjun is married to Kavita. Mohit is Deepa's husband. How is Mohit related to Kavita?

solution.concept: A husband's father is a father-in-law
solution.explanation: Arjun is the son of Deepa and her husband Mohit. Kavita is Arjun's wife, so Mohit is her husband's father: her father-in-law.
steps: Mohit = Arjun's father
Father of one's husband ⇒ father-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Kavita is not Mohit's own child; a brother-in-law would be in Kavita's generation; Grandfather skips a generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'L 4 M 2 N 3 O', how is L related to O?

solution.concept: Decode pair by pair
solution.explanation: L is M's brother; M is N's daughter, so L is also N's son; N is O's wife, so L is O's son.
steps: L 4 M: L is M's brother
M 2 N: M is N's daughter ⇒ L is N's son
N 3 O: N is O's wife ⇒ L is O's son
solution.why_others_wrong: Brother-in-law and Nephew would need L to be outside O's own children; Grandson skips a generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'E 5 F 4 G 1 H', how is F related to H?

solution.concept: A father's brother is an uncle
solution.explanation: E is F's mother; F is G's brother, so F and G are both E's children; G is H's father. F, the brother of H's father, is H's uncle (whether H is a boy or a girl).
steps: E 5 F, F 4 G: F and G are siblings
G 1 H: G is H's father ⇒ F is H's uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: H's father is G; F is a generation above H, so neither H's brother nor cousin.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the expression 'U ? V 2 W', which code should replace ? so that U is definitely the husband of W?

solution.concept: Fix V's parents first
solution.explanation: V is W's daughter. With '1', U is V's father; V has only one father, so W must be V's mother and U, the father of her daughter, is W's husband. With '5', U would be V's mother (W's wife, not husband); with '3' or '4' U is V's wife or brother, which says nothing about U being W's husband.
steps: V 2 W: V is W's daughter
U 1 V: U is V's father ⇒ W is V's mother ⇒ U is W's husband
Test 3, 4, 5: none makes U W's husband
solution.why_others_wrong: '3' makes U V's wife, '4' V's brother and '5' V's mother — none makes U the husband of W.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Fatima related to Ekansh?

solution.concept: Fix both couples first
solution.explanation: Ekansh's father is Gopal, and Chinmay is Gopal's brother. Fatima is Chinmay's wife, so she is the wife of Ekansh's paternal uncle: his aunt.
steps: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh
Fatima = wife of Chinmay = wife of Ekansh's uncle ⇒ aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Ekansh's mother is Hema; Fatima is a generation above Ekansh, so she is not his sister; his grandmother is Bharati.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Chinmay related to Hema?

solution.explanation: Hema is Gopal's wife, and Chinmay is Gopal's brother, so Chinmay is Hema's husband's brother: her brother-in-law.
steps: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh
Hema's husband Gopal; Chinmay = Gopal's brother
solution.why_others_wrong: Hema's husband is Gopal; Anand is her father-in-law; Chinmay is not Hema's own brother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who is Ekansh's father?

solution.concept: Use the 'not an uncle' clue
solution.explanation: Ekansh's father is a son of Anand, i.e. Chinmay or Gopal. The other son would be Ekansh's uncle, and Gopal is not his uncle, so Gopal is the father.

Gopal is not an uncle ⇒ Gopal is the father
solution.why_others_wrong: Chinmay is Ekansh's uncle (Fatima's husband); Anand is his grandfather; the last clue settles it, so it can be determined.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many female members are there in the family?

solution.explanation: Bharati (wife of Anand), Damini (a daughter), Fatima (a wife) and Hema (a mother) are female; Anand, Chinmay, Gopal and Ekansh are male. Four females.

Females: Bharati, Damini, Fatima, Hema

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: A parent's sibling's child is a cousin
solution.explanation: R is S's son; S is T's husband, so T is R's mother; T is U's sister, so U is R's maternal uncle or aunt; U is V's parent, so V is the child of R's mother's sibling: R's cousin (whatever the genders of U and V).
steps: R ▲ S ■ T: R is the son of S and T
T ● U: U is a sibling of R's mother
U ◆ V: V is U's child ⇒ cousin
solution.why_others_wrong: Nephew would put V a generation below R; Brother needs the same parents; Uncle a generation above.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rekha said to Nitin, "Your mother's father-in-law is the only son of my father." How is Rekha related to Nitin?

solution.concept: Collapse the phrase step by step
solution.explanation: Nitin's mother's father-in-law is the father of Nitin's father: Nitin's paternal grandfather. He is the only son of Rekha's father, so he is Rekha's brother. Rekha is therefore the sister of Nitin's grandfather: his grand-aunt.
steps: Mother's father-in-law = father's father = grandfather
Only son of Rekha's father = Rekha's brother
Grandfather's sister ⇒ grand-aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Aunt would be the sister of Nitin's father; Grandmother would be the grandfather's wife, not his sister; Mother-in-law has no basis.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Grand-aunt (sister of his paternal grandfather)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain system, every direction is renamed in the same way: south is called east, east is called north and north is called west. What is west called in that system?

solution.concept: Renaming = turning every direction by the same angle
solution.explanation: South → east is a 90° anticlockwise turn, and so are east → north and north → west. Turning west 90° anticlockwise gives south.
steps: Each name is 90° anticlockwise of the true direction
West turned 90° anticlockwise ⇒ South
solution.why_others_wrong: North turns west the other way; East reverses it; West would mean no renaming at all.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Harsh drives 14 km towards the east. He turns left and drives 9 km, turns left again and drives 6 km, and then turns left once more and drives 3 km. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net east and net north displacement
solution.explanation: He ends 14 − 6 = 8 km east and 9 − 3 = 6 km north of the start: √(64 + 36) = 10 km, north-east.
steps: Start east: 14 km → (14, 0)
Turn left from east ⇒ north: 9 km → (14, 9)
Turn left from north ⇒ west: 6 km → (8, 9)
Turn left from west ⇒ south: 3 km → (8, 6)
√(8² + 6²) = 10 km, North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '10 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '14 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is the school from the market, and in which direction?

solution.concept: A 5-12-13 triangle
solution.explanation: The school is 5 km east and 12 km north of the market: √(25 + 144) = 13 km, north-east.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
School − market = (5, 12)
√(5² + 12²) = 13 km, North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: '13 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '13 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '17 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which place lies on the straight road joining the hospital and the school?

solution.concept: Midpoint test
solution.explanation: The hospital is at (−5, 0) and the school at (5, 12). The midpoint of this segment is (0, 6), exactly where the post office is. The library and the market lie on the line y = 0 and the temple at (0, 12), none of them on the segment.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
Midpoint of hospital and school = (0, 6) = post office
solution.why_others_wrong: The library (−4, 0), the market (0, 0) and the temple (0, 12) are off the hospital–school line.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between the library and the school, and in which direction is the school from the library?

solution.concept: Difference of two positions
solution.explanation: Library (−4, 0), school (5, 12): the school is 9 km east and 12 km north of the library, √(81 + 144) = 15 km, north-east.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
School − library = (9, 12)
√(9² + 12²) = 15 km, North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: '15 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '15 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '21 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is the hospital with respect to the temple?

solution.concept: Signs of the two components
solution.explanation: Hospital (−5, 0) minus temple (0, 12) = (−5, −12): west and south, so the hospital is south-west of the temple.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
Hospital − temple = (−5, −12) ⇒ South-West
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East is the temple's direction from the hospital; South-East takes the hospital as east of the market; West ignores the 12 km north–south gap.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Tina was standing in an open field facing south, and her shadow fell exactly to her right. At what time of the day was this most likely?

options.text: The time cannot be judged from a shadow

solution.concept: A shadow points away from the sun
solution.explanation: Facing south, her right is west, so the shadow pointed west. A shadow points away from the sun, so the sun was in the east: it was morning.
steps: Facing south ⇒ right = west
Shadow west ⇒ sun east ⇒ morning
solution.why_others_wrong: In the evening the sun is in the west and the shadow would fall to her left; at noon the shadow is very short and points north (in India), not west; the side of the shadow does tell the time of day.
solution.final_answer: Option B: In the morning, after sunrise

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Vivaan walks 10 m towards the north. He turns right and walks 5 m, turns right again and walks 4 m, and then turns left and walks 3 m. How far must he walk now, and in which direction, to go straight back to his starting point?

solution.concept: The way back is the opposite of the displacement
solution.explanation: He ends 8 m east and 6 m north of the start, 10 m away. To return he must walk 10 m towards the south-west.
steps: Start north: 10 m → (0, 10)
Turn right from north ⇒ east: 5 m → (5, 10)
Turn right from east ⇒ south: 4 m → (5, 6)
Turn left from south ⇒ east: 3 m → (8, 6)
Displacement (8, 6): 10 m north-east of the start
Way back: 10 m, South-West
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 m, South-East' mixes up east and west; '10 m, North-East' gives the end point's direction from the start; '14 m, South-West' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Kabir and Laila stand back to back, Kabir facing east. Kabir then turns 135° clockwise, and Laila turns 135° anticlockwise. What is the smaller angle between the directions they now face?

solution.concept: Find each new facing, then compare
solution.explanation: Kabir: east + 135° clockwise = south-west. Laila faces west (back to back with Kabir); west − 135° = south-east. South-west and south-east are 90° apart.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° and 135° come from turning one of them the wrong way; 180° assumes they still face opposite ways.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A drone takes off from point O and flies 9 km towards the north. It then turns 45° clockwise and flies 4√2 km, turns 135° clockwise and flies 25 km, and finally turns 90° clockwise and flies 9 km. How far is the drone from O, and in which direction?

solution.concept: A diagonal leg of k√2 moves k along each axis
solution.explanation: North 9 → (0, 9). A 45° clockwise turn points it north-east; 4√2 km moves it 4 km east and 4 km north → (4, 13). Another 135° clockwise makes it face south: 25 km → (4, −12). A 90° clockwise turn makes it face west: 9 km → (−5, −12). Distance √(25 + 144) = 13 km, south-west.
steps: Heading north, 9 → (0, 9)
Heading north-east, 4√2 → (4, 13)
Heading south, 25 → (4, -12)
Heading west, 9 → (-5, -12)
√(5² + 12²) = 13 km, South-West
solution.why_others_wrong: '13 km, South-East' mixes up east and west; '13 km, North-East' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '17 km, South-West' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, PRINT is written as MOFKQ. How is GLOBE written in that code language?

solution.concept: Every letter moves back by the same number of places
solution.explanation: P→M, R→O, I→F, N→K, T→Q: every letter moves 3 places back. G→D, L→I, O→L, B→Y (B, A, Z, Y), E→B: DILYB.
steps: GLOBE −3 ⇒ DILYB
solution.why_others_wrong: JORGH moves every letter forward; DILYC moves E back only 2 places; DJLYB moves L back only 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BAT is written as 26 and FUN is written as 44. How is RICE written in that code?

solution.concept: Sum of positions plus the number of letters
solution.explanation: BAT: 2 + 1 + 20 = 23, plus 3 letters = 26. FUN: 6 + 21 + 14 = 41, plus 3 = 44. RICE: 18 + 9 + 3 + 5 = 35, plus 4 letters = 39.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35 leaves out the number of letters; 43 adds 8 (twice the length); 40 adds 5.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'early'?

solution.concept: Remove the codes of the shared words
solution.explanation: In sentence 1, today = mi (in sentences 1, 2, 3), train = ra (1 and 3) and leaves = ko (1 and 4). The leftover code ve is 'early'.
steps: today = mi; train = ra; leaves = ko
early = ve
solution.why_others_wrong: ko is 'leaves', ra is 'train' and mi is 'today'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'pu'?

solution.concept: Leftover code of a sentence
solution.explanation: Sentence 4 is 'platform leaves at night' = 'pu sa zo ko'. platform = sa (shared with sentence 2), leaves = ko (shared with 1) and night = zo (shared with 3), so pu = at.
steps: platform = sa; leaves = ko; night = zo
pu ⇒ at
solution.why_others_wrong: platform = sa, leaves = ko and night = zo.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'night train'?

solution.concept: Two codes, each from a shared pair of sentences
solution.explanation: night is in sentences 3 and 4, whose only common code is zo. train is in sentences 1 and 3, whose common codes are ra and mi; mi is 'today' (also in sentence 2), so train = ra. 'night train' = 'zo ra'.
steps: night = zo (3 ∩ 4)
train = ra (1 ∩ 3, minus today's mi)
solution.why_others_wrong: le is 'arrives', mi is 'today' and pu is 'at'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: For which of the following words can the code NOT be found with certainty?

The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Is M greater than K?

II. P ≥ K.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: A yes/no question is answered when every allowed case gives the same answer
solution.explanation: I says nothing about K, and II says nothing about M. Together, M ≥ N > P ≥ K, so M > K: the answer is 'yes'.
steps: I alone: K unknown ⇒ not sufficient
II alone: M unknown ⇒ not sufficient
Together: M ≥ N > P ≥ K ⇒ M > K
solution.why_others_wrong: The 'alone' options use one statement only; 'together not sufficient' ignores that the chain closes when both are combined.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Who sits second to the right of P?

I. R sits immediately to the left of P, and T sits third to the right of R.
II. U sits opposite P, and V is an immediate neighbour of U.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Count places from a fixed person
solution.explanation: I: R is one place to P's left, so three places to R's right is two places to P's right — T. Sufficient. II fixes U opposite P and V next to U, but the seat two places to P's right could still be Q, R, S, T or W — not sufficient.
steps: II: seat P + 2 not fixed
solution.why_others_wrong: II alone leaves the seat open, and I alone already answers, so neither 'together' option is right.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: Notice at the entrance of a museum: "Flash photography is not allowed inside the galleries."

Assumptions:
I. Flash photography can harm the exhibits or disturb other visitors in the galleries.
II. Visitors to the museum do not carry cameras or mobile phones.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: A ban on flash photography is issued only because the museum sees some harm in it, to the exhibits or to other visitors (I). If visitors carried no cameras or phones, the notice would be pointless, so II is not assumed.
steps: Ban on flash ⇒ flash is seen as harmful: I implicit
Notice expects cameras to be carried ⇒ II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both accept II, which goes against the purpose of the notice; Neither ignores the reason for a ban.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: A bakery has put up a board: "Fresh bread available from 7 am every day."

Assumptions:
I. Some people want to buy fresh bread early in the morning.
II. The bakery will be able to have fresh bread ready by 7 am every day.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The bakery advertises early bread because it expects buyers at that hour (I), and it would not promise bread from 7 am every day unless it expects to have bread ready by then (II).
steps: Advertising an early hour ⇒ demand expected: I
Promise of bread by 7 am ⇒ able to bake in time: II
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two things the promise rests on; Neither ignores both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

steps: 'Every customer' is an extreme claim ⇒ I not implicit
Quality is not mentioned ⇒ II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I, Only II and Both accept a claim the sign does not need.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is implicit

Statement: Instruction printed on an admit card: "Carry a valid photo identity card. Candidates without one will not be allowed into the examination hall."

Assumptions:
I. Every candidate already has a passport.
II. Some candidates may come to the examination hall without a valid photo identity card.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The warning is printed because the examining body expects that some candidates might forget or not have a valid identity card (II). Many kinds of photo identity card are valid; nothing suggests that every candidate has a passport (I).
steps: Warning ⇒ some may come without an ID: II
Passport for every candidate is not needed ⇒ I not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both accept the passport claim; Neither misses the reason for the warning.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only assumption II is implicit
